resource.name: Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Endline Politician Survey
resource.description: USAID’s Center of Excellence for Democracy, Human Rights and Governance contracted Social Impact, Inc. to conduct an impact evaluation of USAID’s Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanisms (G-SAM) program, which aimed to increase accountability of local District Assemblies in Ghana. This impact evaluation, a randomized-controlled trial, tested the effect of two distinct efforts to increase accountability and improve service delivery outcomes at the district level. One hundred fifty of Ghana’s districts were matched and randomized into one of three groups: a top-down treatment group that received performance audits conducted by the central government Ghana Audit Service (GAS); a bottom-up treatment group that received civil-society organization (CSO) led scorecard campaigns; and a control group that did not receive either intervention. Outcomes were measured across three surveys administered at baseline (2014) and endline (2017). This dataset specifically contains endline data from a survey targeted at district politicians, who make decisions on which development projects to build in which communities.

domain_metadata.value: Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels. 2023. Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Endline Politician Survey. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/chhs-uafd.

As part of the de-identification process, we removed/recoded some geographic variables that may limit usability. In the household datasets, we removed village names and masked enumeration areas to prevent the risk of re-identification; this will prevent users from summarizing data at the village / EA levels, or tracking trends at these levels. Also to prevent the risk of re-identification, in the politician and administrator datasets, we removed district names and masked region names, which will make it impossible to associate responses with specific districts and regions.  Another limitation is that although the household survey was a panel survey, with the same households surveyed at baseline and endline, the household unique identifier is not available. As a result, households cannot be match across rounds and the data must be treated as a repeated cross section, rather than a panel survey.
Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels
Bureau for Development, Democracy, and Innovation

All datasets within this data asset have undergone an extensive de-identification process. The project team has reviewed each of the datasets individually for direct and indirect identifiers, including geographic variables. In consultation with Social Impact’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), we have removed all direct identifiers such as names, phone numbers, and physical addresses, as well as low-level geographic variables such as GPS coordinates, enumeration areas, and village names. We have also removed district names and encoded the region variable for the politician and administrator datasets due to the small number of politicians and administrators in each district and region. In addition, we recoded the age variable (transforming it from continuous to categorical) and recoded minority religious groups identified through the religion variable and minority tribal groups identified through the tribe variable as “Other.” We also reviewed all open-ended text variables and recoded any variables containing responses with potential PII as “missing.” This de-identified data asset has been approved for publication by the Social Impact IRB. Please see the USAID Data Services DDL Variable Manipulation Overview, https://data.usaid.gov/api/views/xw2i-z7hr/files/de8f1fd7-1803-43bf-9a5a-de5f67a57ccb, noting the risk mitigation techniques implemented in some data assets on the DDL, as well as examples of the impact of these techniques on the data.

The data included in this data asset was collected as part of an impact evaluation of the Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanism’s (G-SAM) project, which aimed to improve accountability at the district level in Ghana. We believe this data would be a valuable resource for other researchers studying government accountability and could even be used to inform future good governance interventions across West Africa. The politician and administrator datasets capture information on the education and position of district-level administrators and politicians in Ghana, the perceived importance/ranking of factors that determine political success, factors that influence the types/locations of development projects, the process of identifying contractors for development projects and common issues in the construction or of these projects, perceived government corruption at the district level, the performance and provision of government services, and government accountability. The household datasets contain information on citizens’ views on the quality of services in their district, perceived factors that influence the type and location of development projects, perceived reasons for issues or other delays with projects in their district, the quality of governance and the political environment in their district, their participation in district politics and level of political sophistication, reported factors that influence their vote, perceived government accountability in their district, and levels of social cohesion in their community. Since this data asset contains three baseline datasets and three endline datasets each containing a wide range of variables, researchers who use this data asset will be able to understand changes in the above factors in Ghana over the 3-year period between 2014 and 2017.

resource.name: Feed the Future Senegal: Yaajeende Women's Dietary Data
resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

resource.name: Feed The Future Interim Population-Based Assessment of Cambodia, Module E1-07, Quantity of Food Consumed that Came from Other Sources: Section 1
resource.description: This dataset records the amount of food consumed by the household that came from gifts or other sources during the 7 days before the survey from the first interim assessment of Feed the Future's population-based indicaors for the ZOI in Cambodia.  It has 1019 rows and 768 columns.  The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Niger-- Household Sanitation and Maternal Health
resource.description: This dataset captures data about the mothers in the households surveyed  as part of the Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in the Maradi and Zinder regions in Niger as well as the water and sanitation resources available to the household.  It has 200 columns and 7,337 rows.   In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Niger.  The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions. FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Implementing Partner Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

Although the evaluators did identify participants in the focus groups and key informant interviews, the data that could identify respondents was not included in any of the spreadsheets.

The dataset consists of recorded responses to a series of questions asked during key informant interviews (KII) or client focus groups regarding the delivery of HIV/AIDS related services. There are 11 spreadsheets, each recording the answers of a different set of actors in health service delivery: district health officers, focus groups comprised of clients (two spreadsheets), clinic staff, laboratory staff, implementing partners, lower level facility staff, Ministry of Health staff, regional referral hospital staff, SUSTAIN project staff, and USAID staff.

resource.name: Feed the Future Tanzania Mboga na Matunda Private Sector Survey 2019 - Module B Proprietors
resource.description: This data asset contains data from the beneficiary based fiscal year 2019 annual results survey of private sector firms assisted by the Feed the Future Tanzania - Mboga na Matunda Project. The project works to improve the livelihoods of horticultural farmers in the regions of Iringa, Morogoro, Songwe, Mbeya, and Zanzibar, and strengthen the market system throughout the ZOI. The survey sample was developed using one level of stratification, firm type. Firms were selected from five different categories: Processor, Buyer, Local input supplier, Regional input supplier, Finance provider, and Other service provider. In total, 321 firms were surveyed. The data is split into modules. Module A captures basic identifying data on the firm. Module B captures information on the proprietors. Modules C, D, E, F, G and H capture data on sales of products and services. Module I captures information on business practices. Module J captures information on production costs. Module K captures information on access to finance.

resource.name: Breakthrough ACTION Malaria Behavior Survey - Malawi Women's Dataset
resource.description:
The women's questionnaire dataset is a compiliation of all the responses to the women's questionnaire of the Malaria Behavior Survey. 
This Malaria Behavior Survey (MBS) dataset includes representative data on the determinants of malaria-related behaviors from urban and rural areas in the Northern, Central, and Southern regions of Malawi, collected between May 26th and July 1st 2021. The goal of this study was two-fold: 1) to provide a better understanding of the socio-demographic, attitudinal, and normative characteristics (also referred to as ideational characteristics) associated with malaria-related behavioral outcomes in the Northern, Central, and Southern regions of Malawi and 2) to determine the appropriate focus of programmatic activities designed to improve malaria-related ideational and behavioral outcomes. This study used a cross-sectional survey design with a random sample of women and men using structured questionnaires. Respondents were selected through a multi-step cluster random sampling approach. The research team collected relevant information from 3,862 households, which included 4,181 women of reproductive age and 1,304 of their male spouses/partners.

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda--Maternal Health and Household Sanitation
resource.description: This dataset captures data about the mothers in the households surveyed  as part of the Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda as well as the water and sanitation resources available to the household.  This dataset contains data from Modules F and J of the questionnaire and has 295 columns and 4,766 rows.  In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Uganda.  The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions.  FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.  The data asset is comprised of six datasets: 1) a description of all members of the households surveyed, 2) data on maternal health and sanitation practices, 3) data about the children in the household, 4) data describing the agricultural practices of the household, 5) data describing the food consumption of the household (broken into 4 smaller spreadsheets), and 6) and a description of the weights that should be applied during the analysis of the other datasets.

resource.name: Tusome Kenya 2015 Baseline: Student, Teacher, and Headteacher Data
resource.description: This data file contains student, teacher, and headteacher data from the project's 2015 baseline. The Tusome Early Grade Reading Program involves a national effort in Kenya to scale up a proven model for improved results in early grade literacy. Based on positive findings during a rigorous impact evaluation of a pilot test of this intervention, the Government of Kenya (GOK) asked USAID/Kenya to assist with the nationwide rollout of an activity to improve reading skills and increase the capacity of educators and the GOK to deliver and administer early grade reading (EGR) programs modeled on the pilot activity’s success. Tusome, which means “Let’s Read” in Kiswahili, targeted 28,000 formal and nonformal public and low-cost private primary schools in the 47 counties in Kenya (nationwide). About 1,000 of these are informal schools that exist mostly in urban “slums,” while the vast majority of the remaining 27,000 schools are in rural areas. Roughly 5.4 million children who entered primary school between 2014 and 2017 are expected to benefit from this scaling-up initiative. Intermediate beneficiaries include: 1) approximately 60,000 class 1 and 2 teachers, 2) 28,000 primary school head teachers, 3) 1,052 Teacher Advisory Center (TAC) tutors, plus “coaches” for nonformal schools and 4) 300 senior education personnel. Tusome also assisted the GOK at the technical and policy levels to sustainably improve reading skills beyond the span of the activity.

resource.name: Nepal Business Literacy Impact Evaluation - Baseline Women Dataset
resource.description:
Feed the Future activities in Nepal include the Business Literacy (BL) Program, which operates in conjunction with the Knowledge-Based Integrated Sustainable Agriculture and Nutrition (KISAN) Project. Nepal Business Literacy (BL) Impact Evaluation (IE) is designed to collect and analyze three rounds of qualitative and quantitative data collected in order to learn from evidence of the extent to which initial and persistent results of the BL training course occur. The Nepal BL IE is designed to investigate initial and longer-term or persistent impacts of the training experience on targeted aspects of beneficiaries’ knowledge, skills, attitudes (KSA), and behaviors. Investigators also are interested in whether and to what extent the BL training experience leads to adoption of targeted behaviors, such as starting new micro enterprises, that persist over time.

resource.description: This dataset captures the non-food expenditures over the past 7 days for each household surveyed during the first interim assessment of Feed the Future’s population-based indicators for the ZOI in Cambodia. It has 1019 rows and 579 columns.  The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.

resource.name: A genome‑wide association and meta‑analysis: Common bean syntelogs and their corresponding cowpea genes
resource.description: Seed size is an important trait for yield and commercial value in dry-grain cowpea. Seed size varies widely among different cowpea accessions, and the genetic basis of such variation is not yet well understood. To better decipher the genetic basis of seed size, a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and meta-analysis were conducted on a panel of 368 cowpea diverse accessions from 51 countries. Four traits, including seed weight, length, width and density were evaluated across three locations. Using 51,128 single nucleotide polymorphisms covering the cowpea genome, 17 loci were identified for these traits. One locus was common to weight, width and length, suggesting pleiotropy. By integrating synteny-based analysis with common bean, six candidate genes (Vigun05g036000, Vigun05g039600, Vigun05g204200, Vigun08g217000, Vigun11g187000, and Vigun11g191300) which are implicated in multiple functional categories related to seed size such as endosperm development, embryo development, and cell elongation were identified. These results suggest that a combination of GWAS meta-analysis with synteny comparison in a related plant is an efficient approach to identify candidate gene (s) for complex traits in cowpea. The identified loci and candidate genes provide useful information for improving cowpea varieties and for molecular investigation of seed size.

resource.description: The Power Africa Enabling Environment Tracker 2020 data in the DDL are used in Power Africa's Enabling Environment Tracker dashboard. The Enabling Environment Tracker is an interactive data aggregation and visualization tool that pulls together publicly available data on policy and regulatory trends across Africa’s energy sector into one, easily accessible location. The dataset includes publicly available, third-party data points, which were selected based off Power Africa's Enabling Environment Principles. The principles lay out key elements for increasing private sector investment and doubling electricity access in Sub-Saharan Africa. The hope is that Power Africa's African government partners, private sector partners, development partners, and other stakeholders use the tool to assess enabling environment progress, inform technical assistance interventions, and guide advocacy for needed reforms.

resource.name: FTF Ghana 2015 Interim Population-Based Survey: Individual Leadership and Influence
resource.description: Feed the Future (FTF) initiative in Ghana is a collaborative effort that supports country-owned processes and plans for improving food security and nutrition, particularly in the northern part of the country. These datasets cover the interim survey that took place in 2015 and was designed as a follow-up to the baseline survey that happened from 2012 to 2013. The survey covered a range of indicators organized around four groups: (1) economic well-being; (2) women and children anthropometry; (3) hunger and diet diversity; and (4) women's empowerment. The survey design involved two stages in which enumeration areas were selected followed by households. Data was collected in a face-to-face fashion using well-designed questionnaires and other study materials.

resource.name: Agricultural Land Dynamics and Land Policy in Rural Tanzania 2016: Livestock Products Dataset
resource.description:
This dataset contains information about cost and quantity of products derived from the farm’s livestock. The table can be combined with other datasets in this data asset using the 'hhid' column.

The purpose of collecting these data was to examine farm expansion and labor markets in rural Tanzania. Data were collected in 8 rural districts of Tanzania: Mvomero, Kilombero, Njombe, Kiteto, Magu, Moshi Rural, Mkuranga and Liwale.

The data were collected through the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Food Security Policy (FSP).

agricultural operations on the welfare of rural communities around them.

resource.name: Global Database of Humanitarian Organisations (GDHO) 2021 Data
resource.description:
GDHO is a global compendium of organisations that provide aid in humanitarian crises. The database includes basic organisational and operational information on these humanitarian providers, which include international non-governmental organisations (grouped by federation), national NGOs that deliver aid within their own borders, UN humanitarian agencies, and the International Red Cross and Red Crescent movements. 

All the organisations included in the database have responded to humanitarian needs in at least one emergency context, individually or in partnership with other organisations, even if their stated mission is not strictly humanitarian. Not included are NGOs devoted to development, human rights, or political causes, or that do not work in emergency settings.

There is no sensitive data in this data asset.

Humanitarian Outcomes has launched a newly improved, public version of the Global Database of Humanitarian Organisations (GDHO), providing the humanitarian sector with a centralised source of basic information on providers and resources across the globe. Despite a proliferation of disparate datasets on various humanitarian indicators, the sector as a whole is starved of metadata; that is, basic information about itself. As a result, seemingly straightforward questions about the size of the sector in terms of personnel and resources, and the scope of operations globally and within countries, have been impossible to answer. This is more than just an information problem—the lack of data obscures the gaps in coverage within and across crises and the extent to which the system provides an impartial response according to need. We built the GDHO to help fill this gap. As a regularly updated, publicly accessible database, the GDHO serves three main goals:to provide a clearer picture of the size, operational scope, and composition of global humanitarian resources;to give visibility to the national and local NGOs that play a principal role in humanitarian response yet whose work too often goes unseen; and to better estimate the aid worker population in order to calculate rates in analysis

resource.name: Malawi Baseline Impact Evaluation: Children's Data
resource.description:
Feed the Future initiative in Malawi is committed to improving food security and nutrition in farming households while reducing rural poverty through an agriculture-­led, integrated economic growth, nutrition, and natural resource management strategy. The goal of the impact evaluation is to determine whether integrating nutrition interventions
alongside agricultural value chain interventions will contribute to a greater reduction in malnutrition among children under 3 years of age, compared to nutrition improvements anticipated from stand-­alone value chain activities.

The main objectives are to enable USAID missions to meet the performance monitoring requirements of Feed the Future and maximize the use and benefits of data collected; provide high-­quality empirical evidence to inform program design and investment decisions that will promote sustainable food security; ensure timely availability of high­quality data for use in monitoring performance and evaluating impacts of the Feed the Future initiative; and facilitate accountability and learning about which Feed the Future interventions work best, under what conditions, and at what cost.

We identified variables within the asset that present privacy risk (key variables) and applied the following techniques: a 3-anonymity technique on categorical key variables, such as geographic variables, household size, gender, and age. In order to reach the 3-anonymity threshold, we recoded some variables and suppressed values that increasedthe risk of re-identification. Doing so reduces the precision of the cells, while preserving statistical utility. 3-anonymity mitigates risk on key categorical variables in a combined way.

resource.name: Haiti Sorghum Intercropping Sugarcane Aphid Study 2018-2019 - Natural Enemies Dataset
resource.description: This dataset captures data on natural enemies of aphids, Lacewings (Neuroptera: Chrysopidae) and ladybeetles (Coleoptera: Coccinellid), collected in intercropped experimental plots. It contains 234 rows and 6 columns. Two experiments were conducted, one planted on 8/22/2018 (fall 2018) and another planted on 1/19/2019 (spring 2019), in Jonc-Labeille, Haiti. Three experimental treatments were compared: sorghum, sorghum intercropped with maize, and sorghum intercropped with pigeon pea. The sorghum variety was “Bout gode,” the maize variety was “Chicken corn,” and the pigeon pea was “Pwa kongo local.” A randomized complete block design experiment was used.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Output data for the Sanzi by Vita 7 population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Output data for the Sanzi by Vita 7 population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/e8nu-ixpc.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Coral Data for MINISTRY OF MARINE AFFAIRS AND FISHERIES REPUBLIC OF INDONESIA - Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN)
resource.description:
The narrative of what the data includes follows:  
1.	Data consist of coral coverage. All inputted in the excel following GCRMN instructions which written in the sheet named information in each excel. There are four organizations working with SEA Project in the data survey: WWF (World Wildlife Fund), WCS (Wildlife Conservation Society), CTC (Coral Triangle Center) and CI (Conservation International).

2.	Coral survey using Point Intercept Transect (PIT) methodology with 50 meters length in 3 and 10 meters depth. Coral data cover 11 Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) in East Indonesia supported by SEA Project: in Maluku Province (Buano MPA, Koon MPA, Serutbar MPA, Lease MPA); in North Maluku Province (Guraici MPA, Mare MPA, Dehegila-Rao Bay MPA, Widi MPA and Sula MPA); in West Papua Province (Fakfak Berau Bay MPA and Fakfak Nusalasi Bay MPA). The data is one series that been taken in 2016 or 2017 or 2018. The sampling points in some MPAs are inside the MPA boundaries. Even though it is inside the MPA the condition is actually not protected because the MPA is still not active in term of the management.
columns_description: Method of survey (Quadrat, transect, timed swim or manta tow; indicate specific sampling, e.g. point, line or belt)

resource.name: Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Endline Household Survey
resource.description: USAID’s Center of Excellence for Democracy, Human Rights and Governance contracted Social Impact, Inc. to conduct an impact evaluation of USAID’s Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanisms (G-SAM) program, which aimed to increase accountability of local District Assemblies in Ghana. This impact evaluation, a randomized-controlled trial, tested the effect of two distinct efforts to increase accountability and improve service delivery outcomes at the district level. One hundred fifty of Ghana’s districts were matched and randomized into one of three groups: a top-down treatment group that received performance audits conducted by the central government Ghana Audit Service (GAS); a bottom-up treatment group that received civil-society organization (CSO) led scorecard campaigns; and a control group that did not receive either intervention. Outcomes were measured across three surveys administered at baseline (2014) and endline (2017). This dataset specifically contains endline data from a survey targeted at citizens, whom G-SAM aimed to empower to be better-informed participants in district governance.

domain_metadata.value: Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels. 2023. Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Endline Household Survey. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/ezs9-pf9y.

As part of the de-identification process, we removed/recoded some geographic variables that may limit usability. In the household datasets, we removed village names and masked enumeration areas to prevent the risk of re-identification; this will prevent users from summarizing data at the village / EA levels, or tracking trends at these levels. Also to prevent the risk of re-identification, in the politician and administrator datasets, we removed district names and masked region names, which will make it impossible to associate responses with specific districts and regions.  Another limitation is that although the household survey was a panel survey, with the same households surveyed at baseline and endline, the household unique identifier is not available. As a result, households cannot be match across rounds and the data must be treated as a repeated cross section, rather than a panel survey.
Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels
Bureau for Development, Democracy, and Innovation

All datasets within this data asset have undergone an extensive de-identification process. The project team has reviewed each of the datasets individually for direct and indirect identifiers, including geographic variables. In consultation with Social Impact’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), we have removed all direct identifiers such as names, phone numbers, and physical addresses, as well as low-level geographic variables such as GPS coordinates, enumeration areas, and village names. We have also removed district names and encoded the region variable for the politician and administrator datasets due to the small number of politicians and administrators in each district and region. In addition, we recoded the age variable (transforming it from continuous to categorical) and recoded minority religious groups identified through the religion variable and minority tribal groups identified through the tribe variable as “Other.” We also reviewed all open-ended text variables and recoded any variables containing responses with potential PII as “missing.” This de-identified data asset has been approved for publication by the Social Impact IRB. Please see the USAID Data Services DDL Variable Manipulation Overview, https://data.usaid.gov/api/views/xw2i-z7hr/files/de8f1fd7-1803-43bf-9a5a-de5f67a57ccb, noting the risk mitigation techniques implemented in some data assets on the DDL, as well as examples of the impact of these techniques on the data.

The data included in this data asset was collected as part of an impact evaluation of the Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanism’s (G-SAM) project, which aimed to improve accountability at the district level in Ghana. We believe this data would be a valuable resource for other researchers studying government accountability and could even be used to inform future good governance interventions across West Africa. The politician and administrator datasets capture information on the education and position of district-level administrators and politicians in Ghana, the perceived importance/ranking of factors that determine political success, factors that influence the types/locations of development projects, the process of identifying contractors for development projects and common issues in the construction or of these projects, perceived government corruption at the district level, the performance and provision of government services, and government accountability. The household datasets contain information on citizens’ views on the quality of services in their district, perceived factors that influence the type and location of development projects, perceived reasons for issues or other delays with projects in their district, the quality of governance and the political environment in their district, their participation in district politics and level of political sophistication, reported factors that influence their vote, perceived government accountability in their district, and levels of social cohesion in their community. Since this data asset contains three baseline datasets and three endline datasets each containing a wide range of variables, researchers who use this data asset will be able to understand changes in the above factors in Ghana over the 3-year period between 2014 and 2017.

This data set contains biological information from important coastal mangrove areas situated at the border of, or near the targeted seascapes of the Caribbean Marine Biodiversity Program (CMBP). The overall objective of the USAID Caribbean Marine Biodiversity Program (CMBP) is to reduce threats to marine-coastal biodiversity in priority areas in the Caribbean—including high biodiversity ecosystems such as coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds—to achieve sustained biodiversity conservation, maintain critical ecosystem services, and realize tangible improvements in human wellbeing for communities adjacent to marine managed areas (MMAs). To achieve this objective, the CMBP addresses direct and indirect threats to marine and coastal biodiversity at multiple geographic scales simultaneously. More specifically, the CMBP includes nested and inter-connected actions across four geographic scales: site, seascape, national and regional. Most of the funding and activities are centered on four targeted seascapes: North Coast of Hispaniola (focus on Haiti); Samaná Bay (Dominican Republic);(iii) Pedro Bank and Southwest Coast of Jamaica (Jamaica)(iv) Grenadine Bank (Grenada and St. Vincent and the Grenadines).

resource.name: A genome‑wide association and meta‑analysis: Candidate genes
resource.description: Seed size is an important trait for yield and commercial value in dry-grain cowpea. Seed size varies widely among different cowpea accessions, and the genetic basis of such variation is not yet well understood. To better decipher the genetic basis of seed size, a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and meta-analysis were conducted on a panel of 368 cowpea diverse accessions from 51 countries. Four traits, including seed weight, length, width and density were evaluated across three locations. Using 51,128 single nucleotide polymorphisms covering the cowpea genome, 17 loci were identified for these traits. One locus was common to weight, width and length, suggesting pleiotropy. By integrating synteny-based analysis with common bean, six candidate genes (Vigun05g036000, Vigun05g039600, Vigun05g204200, Vigun08g217000, Vigun11g187000, and Vigun11g191300) which are implicated in multiple functional categories related to seed size such as endosperm development, embryo development, and cell elongation were identified. These results suggest that a combination of GWAS meta-analysis with synteny comparison in a related plant is an efficient approach to identify candidate gene (s) for complex traits in cowpea. The identified loci and candidate genes provide useful information for improving cowpea varieties and for molecular investigation of seed size.

The data and metadata that comprise this open access, peer-reviewed technical publication provide guidance on genetic variability related to seed size in cowpea. Seed size is an important aspect of consumer preferences, thus also an important aspect of the development of new cowpea varieties through breeding. The information in this publication describes reliable genetic markers to track genetic variants for seed size in parents and progeny.

resource.description: The baseline survey in Tajikistan captures data in the Feed the Future Zones of Influence (ZOI), comprised of 12 of the 24 districts in Khatlon province. The survey is comprised of ten CSV files: a children's file, a household-level file, a household member level file, a women's file, several files describing consumption, and two files used to construct the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index. resource.name: Farm Plots Survey for Agriculture for Children's Empowerment (ACE) in Liberia- Workforce Baseline Dataset
resource.description:
The STRIVE project, funded by USAID's Displaced Children and Orphans Fund (DCOF) and managed by FHI 360, used market-led economic strengthening initiatives to improve the well-being of vulnerable children. Through STRIVE, ACDI/VOCA  implemented the Agriculture for Children’s Empowerment (ACE) Project in Liberia, which is founded on the premise that increased household economic security will stimulate more consistent investments in children’s well being via longer term social investments in education and nutrition.  ACE’s primary focus was on the horticulture value chain (VC) — the production and marketing of vegetables by smallholder farmers in Montserrado, Bong, and Nimba counties of Liberia. ACE also strengthened smallholder rice farming to increase household food security using a market-sensitive approach to rice seed lending and cultivation.

This dataset contains information about the workforce described in the survey.

We have used the following steps to anonymize the datasets:1. Remove location variables such as county and Village and retain District 2. Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables sex, occupation, relationship to household head, education, dwelling characteristics, and District. To achieve the threshold of k=3, we will recode variables occupation, relationship to household head, education, dwelling characteristics, and District into broader categories 3. Aggregate or recode variables such as Age (into 10 years categories), diploma (any diploma above high school into other), and grade (into Primary, Junior High, and Senior High)4. Top code variables such as household size (15+ at baseline and 17+ at Endline) and rent paid. 5. Remove direct identifiers (names and cell phone numbers); remove probing variables such as Other-specify when they contain individuals’ names or reference to individuals with a status of refugee.

This data asset contains information about each plot the household owns, their size, the crops grown on them and the methods used to grow plants on those plots. Baseline and endline surveys were conducted in 2011 and 2013, respectively. Each survey generated 6 datasets including a household dataset, a members’ dataset, and other datasets related to Farm, Fertilization, Harvest, and Workforce.

resource.name: Rift Valley Fever Innovation Lab: Rift Valley fever vaccine animal testing data at Sante Animale MCI in Mohammedia, Morocco
resource.description: The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of a live, attenuated recombinant RVF arMP-12ΔNSm21/384 nucleotide deletion vaccine candidate in domestic ruminants. . The immunogenicity of 2 doses of 104 and 105 Tissue Culture Infectious Doses50% (TCID50) of the vaccine was assessed in of 2 groups of 10 sheep, 2 groups of 10 goats, and doses of 105 and 106 TCID50 were used to vaccinate 2 groups of 10 calves. The results showed that the immunogenicity among sheep, goats and cattle indicated that doses of 104 -   106 TCID50  elicited detectable antibody by day 7 post-vaccination and antibody titers that ranged from 1:14 to 1:305 on day 14 PV with sustained titers through day 28 PV. Overall, these findings indicated that the RVF arMP-12ΔNSm21/384 vaccine is a promising candidate for the prevention of RVF among domestic ruminants.

resource.name: Effect of Participatory Video Extension on Adoption of Drought-Tolerant Maize, Kenya: Pre Intervention Survey
resource.description: A field experiment was conducted in February 2016 in Machakos and Makueni Counties in Kenya aimed at testing methods to increase farmer adoption of drought tolerant (DT) maize varieties, including a participatory video intervention as well as having the video supported by a series of phone-based audio reminders. A list of 50 villages were provided by Farm Input Promotions-Africa (FIPS), an agricultural service provider, including 41 where FIPS was active and 9 where they were not. The 9 villages unsupported by FIPS were all included, and 18 of the supported villages were randomly chosen to be in the study. These 27 villages were randomly assigned to one of three groups: control, video only, and video plus audio reminders. Thirty maize farmers in the non-FIPS villages (which had a larger population, and 17 farmers in the FIPS villages) were randomly chosen and were surveyed before and after an intervention to see if knowledge of and adoption of DT maize varieties were impacted. The primary intervention was a participatory video screened in a set of villages that educated farmers about DT maize varieties including appropriate planting and growing techniques. A narrative/story-telling film shot in the region was used featuring local farmer-actors speaking in the local dialect (Kamba). Following the screening, a moderated discussion was held to reinforce information from the video. In the video plus audio group, a series of four follow-up audio reminders were sent to farmers' mobile phones at key points in the season. Farmers in the control group of villages received no video or audio interventions. The baseline survey was completed in early February 2016, the video screenings took place in late February, and the follow-up survey on the same households was completed in September 2016. A full description of theory, method, and results can be found in Cai, Tian. "Knowledge, Risk, and Benefit Perceptions: Using Participatory Video and Tailored Mobile Messages to Motivate Farmers' Uptake of Drought Tolerant (DT) Maize Seed in Kenya." Order No. 10689089 Michigan State University, East Lansing, 2017: ProQuest.

resource.name: Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 2 Farmers Data
resource.description:
The United States Agency for International Development (USAID)/Pakistan-funded Safe Charity campaign seeks to reduce financial support to violent extremist groups by educating those who give charity about how to direct their charity to safe recipients in Multan and Karachi. In Multan, the campaign trained influential farmers to disseminate safe charity messages to other farmers; and chambers of commerce and industry, trade and marketing associations, and the Rotary Club to reach the business community. In Karachi, the campaign engaged community youth centers to disseminate messages. The campaign timed its activities to align with common periods of charitable giving, namely Ramazan, Eid ul-Fitr, and Eid ul-Azha. 

These surveys established a baseline of current knowledge and practices with respect to safe charity in Multan and Karachi during each giving period and identified changes in knowledge and practices that could be plausibly linked to the safe charity campaign.

domain_tags: institute of social and policy sciences

domain_metadata.value: Management Systems International (MSI). 2020. Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 2 Farmers Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/fcyc-8vij.

The assessment conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. The primary limitation to the data from the Phase I survey was a snowball sampling approach to identifying survey respondents who had been exposed to safe charity messaging. For example, the survey team relied on farmer leaders, who had directly engaged with the safe charity campaign, to identify other members of farmer communities with knowledge of safe charity activities. While it was necessary to include “secondary” farmers in the survey sample to assess the reach of safe charity messaging within target communities, the survey team could not guarantee that secondary farmers had participated in safe charity activities or been exposed to safe charity messaging. Furthermore, there is a high likelihood of a selection bias in farmer leader referrals. To control for this bias, the survey team identified enough secondary farmers to create a secondary sampling frame, from which respondents could be randomly selected. The primary limitation to the survey of members of the business community was lack of familiarity with the safe charity campaign, particularly among corporate businesses. This may have been due to challenges identifying knowledgeable individuals within corporate businesses, lower levels of engagement between corporate businesses and their respective chambers of commerce, or characteristics of the corporate engagement strategy of the safe charity campaign.  Whereas the Phase I surveys focused on the giving of zakat and fitrana, the Phase II survey focused specifically on safe charity practices for the giving of qurbani. Phase II included only farmers and excluded the business community and Karachi youth center participants. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign.

All unique individual identifiers, including names, addresses, and phone numbers of respondents, as well as names of data collection and processing teams, have been removed from the CRA Safe Charity study dataset and omitted from the final report. A unique identification code has been assigned to each survey respondent, reflecting the respondent’s geographic location (city), type of respondent (direct/indirect, farmers/businessman/workshop participants) and sex. The dataset does include information pertaining to respondents’ sex, educational attainment, religion, employment status, and income, which are important variables to explain variation in responses. These variables, however, together do not provide sufficient information to identify individual respondents.

The assessment team, led by MSI and the Institute of Social and Policy Sciences (I-SAPS), conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I, which took place in August 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II, which took place in October 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. Phase I included three surveys, each targeting a unique respondent group. In Multan, the assessment team selected a random sample of 124 farmer “leaders” from 500 farmers in 11 union councils who were directly engaged by the safe charity campaign. Farmer leaders were pre-identified influential members of their communities, tasked with disseminating information to other farmers and community members through community gatherings, sensitization sessions, and other activities and events. The sample of farmer leaders was stratified by gender and union council. With assistance from farmer leaders, the assessment team then used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of at least 500 “secondary” farmers, or members of target communities who participated in community gatherings, sensitizations sessions, and other activities and events sponsored by the safe charity campaign. Using this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 150 secondary farmers, also stratified by gender and union council. The assessment team conducted a second Phase I survey of members of chambers of commerce and industry in Multan. The team randomly selected 150 businesses—120 members (40 corporate members and 80 associate members) of the Multan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MCCI), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 1,000 businesses at the time of the survey; and 30 businesses from the Women Chamber of Commerce and Industry Multan (WCCIM), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 140 businesses at the time of the survey. The assessment team conducted a third Phase I survey of all 103 participants of safe charity poster workshops conducted at Azm-e-Naujawan (AeN) community youth centers. The campaign expected another 850 community members to attend AeN safe charity poster exhibits. Through AeN center staff and poster workshop participants, the assessment team used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of approximately 400 visitors to the poster exhibitions. From this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 121 exhibit visitors, stratified by gender. As with secondary farmers, the snowball approach to identifying secondary participants could not ensure activity participation or exposure to safe charity messaging, and may have been subject to a selection bias. The Phase II survey focused solely on farmer leaders and secondary farmers in Multan. During Phase II, the assessment team surveyed 124 farmer leaders, 112 of whom were surveyed in Phase I and 12 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Similarly, the assessment team surveyed 152 secondary farmers, 131 of whom were also surveyed in Phase 1, and 21 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Together, these surveys provide a comprehensive snapshot of how people in these communities give charity and the role that the risk of giving to violent extremist groups plays in charitable decision-making. The surveys captured three types of information. First, they probed how people give charity, including frequency of giving, type of giving, who in the household makes charitable giving decisions, why people give charity, and factors determining to whom people give charity. Second, the surveys probed people’s knowledge of the risk of giving to violent extremist groups, where people obtain information about safe charity, and how this knowledge affects decision-making. Third, the surveys probed participation in safe charity activities and the effect of this participation on knowledge and behaviors, including further dissemination of safe charity messaging. The survey data can be disaggregated by gender, age, income, religion, and respondent type, as well as period of charitable giving. The two phases of data collection provide important insights into how hyperlocal conditions of place and time affect charitable decision-making and knowledge and practice of safe charity. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. resource.name: Feed the Future Senegal: Yaajeende Household Data
resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Phenotype data for the minicore population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Phenotype data for the minicore population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/fimp-qvdy.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 1 Workshop Data
resource.description:
The United States Agency for International Development (USAID)/Pakistan-funded Safe Charity campaign seeks to reduce financial support to violent extremist groups by educating those who give charity about how to direct their charity to safe recipients in Multan and Karachi. In Multan, the campaign trained influential farmers to disseminate safe charity messages to other farmers; and chambers of commerce and industry, trade and marketing associations, and the Rotary Club to reach the business community. In Karachi, the campaign engaged community youth centers to disseminate messages. The campaign timed its activities to align with common periods of charitable giving, namely Ramazan, Eid ul-Fitr, and Eid ul-Azha. 

These surveys established a baseline of current knowledge and practices with respect to safe charity in Multan and Karachi during each giving period and identified changes in knowledge and practices that could be plausibly linked to the safe charity campaign.

domain_metadata.value: Management Systems International (MSI). 2020. Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 1 Workshop Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/fisz-2f66.

The assessment conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. The primary limitation to the data from the Phase I survey was a snowball sampling approach to identifying survey respondents who had been exposed to safe charity messaging. For example, the survey team relied on farmer leaders, who had directly engaged with the safe charity campaign, to identify other members of farmer communities with knowledge of safe charity activities. While it was necessary to include “secondary” farmers in the survey sample to assess the reach of safe charity messaging within target communities, the survey team could not guarantee that secondary farmers had participated in safe charity activities or been exposed to safe charity messaging. Furthermore, there is a high likelihood of a selection bias in farmer leader referrals. To control for this bias, the survey team identified enough secondary farmers to create a secondary sampling frame, from which respondents could be randomly selected. The primary limitation to the survey of members of the business community was lack of familiarity with the safe charity campaign, particularly among corporate businesses. This may have been due to challenges identifying knowledgeable individuals within corporate businesses, lower levels of engagement between corporate businesses and their respective chambers of commerce, or characteristics of the corporate engagement strategy of the safe charity campaign.  Whereas the Phase I surveys focused on the giving of zakat and fitrana, the Phase II survey focused specifically on safe charity practices for the giving of qurbani. Phase II included only farmers and excluded the business community and Karachi youth center participants. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign.

All unique individual identifiers, including names, addresses, and phone numbers of respondents, as well as names of data collection and processing teams, have been removed from the CRA Safe Charity study dataset and omitted from the final report. A unique identification code has been assigned to each survey respondent, reflecting the respondent’s geographic location (city), type of respondent (direct/indirect, farmers/businessman/workshop participants) and sex. The dataset does include information pertaining to respondents’ sex, educational attainment, religion, employment status, and income, which are important variables to explain variation in responses. These variables, however, together do not provide sufficient information to identify individual respondents.

The assessment team, led by MSI and the Institute of Social and Policy Sciences (I-SAPS), conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I, which took place in August 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II, which took place in October 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. Phase I included three surveys, each targeting a unique respondent group. In Multan, the assessment team selected a random sample of 124 farmer “leaders” from 500 farmers in 11 union councils who were directly engaged by the safe charity campaign. Farmer leaders were pre-identified influential members of their communities, tasked with disseminating information to other farmers and community members through community gatherings, sensitization sessions, and other activities and events. The sample of farmer leaders was stratified by gender and union council. With assistance from farmer leaders, the assessment team then used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of at least 500 “secondary” farmers, or members of target communities who participated in community gatherings, sensitizations sessions, and other activities and events sponsored by the safe charity campaign. Using this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 150 secondary farmers, also stratified by gender and union council. The assessment team conducted a second Phase I survey of members of chambers of commerce and industry in Multan. The team randomly selected 150 businesses—120 members (40 corporate members and 80 associate members) of the Multan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MCCI), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 1,000 businesses at the time of the survey; and 30 businesses from the Women Chamber of Commerce and Industry Multan (WCCIM), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 140 businesses at the time of the survey. The assessment team conducted a third Phase I survey of all 103 participants of safe charity poster workshops conducted at Azm-e-Naujawan (AeN) community youth centers. The campaign expected another 850 community members to attend AeN safe charity poster exhibits. Through AeN center staff and poster workshop participants, the assessment team used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of approximately 400 visitors to the poster exhibitions. From this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 121 exhibit visitors, stratified by gender. As with secondary farmers, the snowball approach to identifying secondary participants could not ensure activity participation or exposure to safe charity messaging, and may have been subject to a selection bias. The Phase II survey focused solely on farmer leaders and secondary farmers in Multan. During Phase II, the assessment team surveyed 124 farmer leaders, 112 of whom were surveyed in Phase I and 12 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Similarly, the assessment team surveyed 152 secondary farmers, 131 of whom were also surveyed in Phase 1, and 21 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Together, these surveys provide a comprehensive snapshot of how people in these communities give charity and the role that the risk of giving to violent extremist groups plays in charitable decision-making. The surveys captured three types of information. First, they probed how people give charity, including frequency of giving, type of giving, who in the household makes charitable giving decisions, why people give charity, and factors determining to whom people give charity. Second, the surveys probed people’s knowledge of the risk of giving to violent extremist groups, where people obtain information about safe charity, and how this knowledge affects decision-making. Third, the surveys probed participation in safe charity activities and the effect of this participation on knowledge and behaviors, including further dissemination of safe charity messaging. The survey data can be disaggregated by gender, age, income, religion, and respondent type, as well as period of charitable giving. The two phases of data collection provide important insights into how hyperlocal conditions of place and time affect charitable decision-making and knowledge and practice of safe charity. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign. The surveys are supplemented by in-depth individual and group interviews with primary and secondary safe charity participants.

resource.description: This dataset describes the children and their health interviewed as part of Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in the Maradi and Zinder regions in Niger.  It has 151 columns and 11,030 rows.   In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Niger. The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions. FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.

resource.name: Feed the Future Senegal: Yaajeende Children's Data
resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

resource.name: Comparison of four bacteriophages exposed to chlorine on stainless steel: complete data
resource.description:
The 2014 West African Ebola virus disease outbreak was the largest to date, and conflicting, chlorine-­based surface disinfection protocols to interrupt disease transmission were recommended. We identified only one study documenting surface disinfection efficacy against the Ebola virus, showing a >6.6 log reduction after 5­-minute exposure to 0.5% sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) based on small­-scale tests (Cook et al. (2015)). In preparation for future extensive, large­-scale disinfection efficacy experiments, we replicated the Cook et al. experiment using four potential BSL­-1 surrogates selected based on similarities to the Ebola virus: bacteriophages MS2, M13, Phi6, and PR772. Each bacteriophage was exposed to 0.1% and 0.5% NaOCl for 1, 5, and 10 minutes on stainless steel. MS2 and M13 were only reduced by 3.4 log and 3.5 log after a 10-­minute exposure to 0.5% NaOCl, and would be overly conservative surrogates. Conversely, PR772 was too easily inactivated for surrogate use, as it was reduced by >4.8 log after only 1­-minute exposure to 0.5% NaOCl. Phi6 was slightly more resistant than the Ebola virus, with 4.1 log reduction after a 5­-minute exposure and not detected after a 10-­minute exposure to 0.5% NaOCl. We therefore recommend
Phi6 as a surrogate for evaluating the efficacy of chlorine-­based surface disinfectants against the Ebola virus.
